title: New Materialism and Haraway
keyWorks: J. Bennett, The Enchantment of Modern Life (2001)
D. Haraway, The Companion Species Manifesto (2003)
D. Haraway, Staying with the Trouble (2016)
summary: New materialism is a current of philosophy from the 2000s and 2010s that invites us to look at matter afresh: not as passive raw material but as something lively, active, capable of making a difference. Jane Bennett speaks of "vibrant matter" and "thing-power", while Donna Haraway, who is close to this current, writes about our kinship with other species and about the need to "stay with the trouble" of our time, fleeing neither into despair nor into faith in a miraculous rescue.
onEmotions: For new materialism, feelings are not purely inner, "spiritual" events. They arise in assemblages (Bennett borrows the term from Deleuze) made of the body, food, weather, things, other people and creatures. This lifts part of the load from you: your mood is not only your "achievement" or your "fault". Bennett especially values "enchantment" — a sense of wonder at the world which, she believes, nourishes ethical generosity. Haraway stresses that the hard feelings of our time are better lived through together, in kinship with others, by cultivating "response-ability" — the capacity to respond.

anxiety.text: Spiders, corals, pigeons — Donna Haraway teaches us to think with creatures that live on damaged ground and still weave their webs. Her book Staying with the Trouble is written for anyone who feels the world is falling apart and the future is closed — which includes your anxiety. She criticises two familiar reactions: the belief that technology or someone else will save us, and the weary "there's nothing to be done anymore". Both, for Haraway, lead us away from the present. Instead she proposes "staying with the trouble" — being here, in a tangled, unsettled world, together with other beings, doing what is possible. Then anxiety needs neither to be inflated into the end of the world nor to be silenced. You can bring it back into the present: notice that you are already here, among the living, and that there is a small thing that makes sense right now.
anxiety.practice: Step outside or go to a window for five minutes and find one living creature that is "staying with the trouble" right now: a bird, a roadside tree, grass in a crack in the asphalt. Keep it company in this day.

quote.text: Staying with the trouble requires learning to be truly present, not as a vanishing pivot between awful or edenic pasts and apocalyptic or salvific futures, but as mortal critters entwined in myriad unfinished configurations of places, times, matters, meanings.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

fear.text: Bread, rain, the wires above the street — Jane Bennett sees the world as a noisy assembly where everyone has a voice. Fear makes us shrink and wall ourselves off, as if we were alone against everything. In Vibrant Matter she shows that the world is full of forces that don't obey our control: power grids, food, weather, even trash have what she calls "thing-power". We are not the only ones who act; action is distributed among many participants. This might sound unsettling, but there is relief in it too. Through this lens, you don't have to hold the whole world under control on your own — that is impossible for anyone. You can acknowledge fear as the natural response of a creature among many forces. And then ask yourself: which of these forces are holding me up? Things can be a support as well — a warm blanket, a cup of tea, the ground under your feet.
fear.practice: Find three things around you that are literally holding you right now — the floor, the back of a chair, a mug. Touch each one and say to yourself: "You're taking part too."

quote.text: The capacity of things — edibles, commodities, storms, metals — not only to impede or block the will and designs of humans but also to act as quasi agents or forces with trajectories, propensities, or tendencies of their own.
quote.author: Jane Bennett

sadness.text: A cloudy November day, a short night's sleep, an empty flat — Jane Bennett would say that all of these take part in your mood. So even sadness, usually thought of as purely inner, "in my soul", can be seen more broadly. She writes that a human being is an "assemblage", made of many elements: the body, bacteria, food, light, things and relationships. She discusses, for example, how what we eat can affect mood — as if matter itself takes part in our feelings. It follows that sadness is not proof of your failure but the state of a whole assemblage you are part of: a lack of sunlight, a tired body, a loss, the weather may all be involved. This doesn't diminish the feeling; it makes it more understandable and gentler. And it offers a hint: sometimes the assemblage can be shifted a little very simply — by stepping into the light or spending time near something alive.
sadness.practice: Change one element of the assemblage right now: step into daylight or open a window for five minutes. Notice whether the light takes part in your mood.

grief.text: Hawaiian crows, dying corals — Donna Haraway mourns vanishing species and insists that grieving is important work, not weakness. Grief is love's answer to loss, and it needs room. Following the philosopher Thom van Dooren, she says that mourning helps us understand how deeply we are entangled with others. For Haraway, what has gone does not vanish without a trace: in her images, all living things "compost" one another, passing on matter, stories and connections. She even says that "we are compost, not posthuman". If we follow this thought further, your grief is part of a long thread that binds you to what you have lost, and through it to the living. You can let mourning be shared and slow, without hurrying to "finish" it alone.
grief.practice: Tell someone one small memory of what you have lost — not the whole story, just one detail. This is how mourning becomes shared.

loneliness.text: For Donna Haraway, a pigeon on the roof, the dog you train with, the neighbour on your landing can all become kin: kinship doesn't have to be by blood. Loneliness tells you that you are missing connection — an important truth, and one you can work with. In Staying with the Trouble she calls on us to "make kin" — with friends, neighbours, a chosen family, and also with animals, plants and places. Earlier, in The Companion Species Manifesto, she described how people and dogs have shaped each other over centuries. The new materialists would probably say that loneliness is not a final state but an invitation to new connections, sometimes unusual ones. Kinship can be not only received but woven: from a regular walk, from caring for a plant, from a short conversation with someone you see every day.
loneliness.practice: Make one gesture of kinship today: water a plant, feed the birds, greet by name someone you see every day.

quote.text: We become-with each other or not at all.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

anger.text: Felled forests, poisoned rivers — Donna Haraway writes about them without any sweetness, and there is plenty of anger in her books. Anger often flares up when we see injustice, and there is truth in it. Haraway doesn't ask us to suppress it. But she offers a particular turn — towards "response-ability". It's a play on words: responsibility, and the ability to respond. For Haraway, what matters is not only naming the guilty but learning to respond: what can I do, whom can I join, whom can I care for? In other words, anger can be respected as energy and directed into a response. This doesn't cancel the anger but makes it fruitful: it stops burning you from within and becomes a bond with those you want to protect.
anger.practice: Walk briskly for five minutes and with every step ask: whom do I want to respond to with this anger? By the end of the walk, choose one small act of response.

shame.text: "I would rather be a cyborg than a goddess," Donna Haraway concludes her famous manifesto. Shame rests on the opposite dream: to be a whole, separate, flawless "self". Jane Bennett shows that a person is an assemblage, made of many elements, many of which are beyond your control: bacteria, hormones, environment, the things around you. Back in A Cyborg Manifesto, Donna Haraway wrote that we are all hybrids, mixtures of the organic and the technical, the natural and the cultural — and she saw in this not a flaw but a possibility. In effect, the ideal of a person in full control of themselves is a fantasy. You don't have to answer for every movement of your feelings and body as if you were their sole master. This doesn't cancel responsibility, but it can loosen shame's grip: you are a living tangle, not a statue.
shame.practice: Imagine yourself not as a statue but as a coral reef — a living tangle of thousands of creatures. Ask: what forces besides my will took part in what I'm ashamed of? Name at least two.

guilt.text: Who is to blame when a tree falls on the power lines: the wind, the tree itself, or the lineman who didn't trim the branches? Jane Bennett asks such questions seriously, and they bring relief to guilt — the sense that the consequences of your actions matter to you. She suggests seeing action as distributed: almost any event — from a power outage to an illness — happens through an assemblage of many participants, human and non-human. In Vibrant Matter she examines a major blackout in the power grid that had no single culprit. Then the guilt you carry entirely on your own shoulders is often actually shared among many forces. Bennett doesn't release people from responsibility, but she invites us to see it more modestly and precisely: you are one of the participants, not the sole author. This understanding helps you move from self-punishment to the question: which part of this is mine to change?
guilt.practice: Draw the situation like a blackout diagram: circles for the participants — people, circumstances, things — and arrows for influences. Outline only your own circle and think about what in it can be changed.

envy.text: In cat's cradle, the pattern on your fingers can be passed on but not won — Donna Haraway builds a whole philosophy on this children's game. Envy grows from a completely different picture: life as a competition between separate individuals, who has more and who is more successful. She speaks of "sympoiesis" — "making-with": nothing living makes itself; everything comes about together with others, in entanglements. Through this lens, someone else's success is also a pattern woven by many hands, not a personal victory over you. Envy doesn't disappear, but it softens. You can ask yourself: which patterns am I part of? Where is my thread already holding something important?
envy.practice: Ask someone close to you: "Where do you think my thread is holding something?" Listen to the answer — sometimes the pattern is clearer from outside.

emptiness.text: Max Weber declared the world "disenchanted", and Jane Bennett objected: the magic hasn't gone anywhere, it has just grown quiet. Emptiness and apathy feel as though the world has lost its colour. In The Enchantment of Modern Life she shows in detail why modernity is not stripped of mystery and wonder at all. She shows that enchantment — surprise, a slight shock at the extraordinary within the ordinary — is still possible: in nature, in the city, in words, even in technology. Bennett believes this feeling is not a luxury but a source of energy from which generosity and care for others grow. It follows that emptiness doesn't need to be filled right away with grand meanings. You can begin with the smallest encounter with matter — a smell, a texture, a sound — which gently reminds you that the world is still alive.
emptiness.practice: For thirty seconds, stay with one sensation — the texture of fabric, a sound outside, the taste of water — as if meeting it for the first time. Don't look for meaning; just let the thing act on you.

confusion.text: An octopus thinks with its whole body: most of its neurons are in its arms, and each arm feels out the world on its own. Donna Haraway suggests learning from such creatures precisely when familiar divisions — living and non-living, self and world, nature and culture — stop working and you feel lost. The physicist and philosopher Karen Barad speaks of "intra-action": things don't first exist separately; they take shape through their interaction. Donna Haraway proposes "tentacular thinking" — thinking not in straight lines but in curves, like a creature with tentacles feeling its way through the world. If we follow this thought further, confusion is not a failure but a possible beginning of such thinking. When you don't know where the boundaries lie, you may be closer to reality than someone who is sure of everything. You can let yourself feel your way through the situation little by little, without demanding a clear map right away.
confusion.practice: Close your eyes and explore one object nearby by touch, like an octopus with its arm, without naming it. Then ask the situation an equally "feeling-out" question: what can I learn about it in the next hour?

fatigue.text: A wire overheats, a bridge hums, metal "fatigues" — Jane Bennett admires the stubbornness of matter: things have their limits and announce them. Tiredness and burnout are the same kind of signal: the body can no longer keep up the pace it has been given. New materialism suggests treating the body as a full participant, not as a tool commanded by the will. Jane Bennett writes about "thing-power" — the capacity of matter to resist, to dig in its heels, to act in its own way. Following Spinoza, she speaks of "conatus" — the striving of every body to preserve itself. The new materialists would probably say that your exhaustion is the voice of the matter you are made of, and it deserves respect, not to be overcome. Your body, too, needs to preserve itself. Rest, then, is not laziness or weakness of will but cooperation with your own matter: you listen to it rather than argue with it.
fatigue.practice: Lie on the floor and give it your whole weight, as you would to a reliable support. For five minutes do nothing — let matter recover at its own pace.

boredom.text: How many times have you walked past your own windowsill without ever really looking at it? Boredom appears when the world seems flat and predictable, and Jane Bennett offers an antidote — "enchantment". For her it isn't fairy-tale magic but an entirely real feeling: a brief moment of stillness when something extraordinary suddenly shows through the familiar. Bennett believes enchantment can be cultivated — by slowing down, looking closely, allowing yourself to be surprised. In Vibrant Matter she recalls how she once noticed a chance gathering of things on a storm drain grate — a work glove, pollen, a bottle cap, a stick — and they suddenly seemed to her shimmering and alive. In other words, boredom is not a property of the world but a tiredness of the eye. You can give the world a chance to surprise you.
boredom.practice: Find a random cluster of small things nearby — on the desk, on the windowsill — and describe it aloud like an archaeologist describing a find: what is it, where did it come from, who lived here?

quote.text: To be enchanted is to be struck and shaken by the extraordinary that lives amid the familiar and the everyday.
quote.author: Jane Bennett

joy.text: The first cherries of the season, the smell of rain on asphalt — Jane Bennett would say these are not trifles but small enchantments. For new materialism, joy is not just a pleasant state but a force. Bennett argues that the joy of encountering the world — enchantment — nourishes ethics: to care for the world, you need at least sometimes to delight in it. Without this, she believes, moral demands turn into a heavy duty. Donna Haraway, for her part, writes with humour and playfulness even about the most serious things and calls her work a game of string figures. In effect, joy is not frivolity against a backdrop of trouble but fuel for care. You can let yourself rejoice without holding back — in an animal nearby, a patch of sunlight on the floor, the taste of an apple — and know that this joy makes you a more alive participant in the shared world.
joy.practice: Tell someone what delighted you today, with all the material details — colour, smell, sound. Shared enchantment feeds care.

love.text: For years Donna Haraway went out onto the agility field with her dog Cayenne and wrote that they taught each other — with paws, hands and glances. Love and tenderness are central themes for her. In The Companion Species Manifesto she shows that love between species is not sentimentality but serious, bodily, sometimes difficult work of mutual learning. For Haraway, to love is to "become-with": you change alongside another, and they change alongside you. No one stays the same. Then tenderness is not a fixed state but a shared process that requires attention to who the other really is, not who you imagine them to be. This helps you accept the hard sides of love too — the mismatches, the adjusting to each other, the work. All of this is part of becoming together.
love.practice: For a minute, watch the one you love — a person or an animal — as if seeing them for the first time: how they move, what they notice. Find one trait you haven't seen before.

gratitude.text: Try to count how many beings took part in your morning — and you'll lose count by the coffee. Gratitude is the recognition that you did not make yourself, and new materialism shows how literally true this is. Donna Haraway speaks of "sympoiesis" — making-with: living things are made together, in webs of interdependence, from the bacteria in your gut to the people who raised you. Jane Bennett adds that things take part in our lives too: bread, water, sunlight are not passive resources but co-participants. Through this lens, gratitude is not only politeness towards people but attention to the whole assemblage that supports you. You can silently thank the chair that holds you and the water you drink — not in a magical sense, but as a way of noticing that you are woven into a living world.
gratitude.practice: Touch three non-human participants in your day — a chair, a cup, a sunny windowsill — and silently say "thank you" to each. It's not magic, just a way of noticing the assemblage.

hope.text: "It matters what stories tell stories," Donna Haraway likes to repeat. For her, hope is not the belief that everything will sort itself out but a choice of stories. In Staying with the Trouble she criticises both technological optimism and apocalyptic despair. She proposes the notion of the "Chthulucene" — named after the spider Pimoa cthulhu and the Greek word "chthonic", meaning of the earth, underground. This is her name for a time in which humans and other beings learn to live and recover together, amid damaged places. Hope here is modest and practical: in small communities, in restoration projects, in stories about surviving together. Haraway especially values stories, because they shape which worlds we will be able to build. It follows that to hope is to choose and tell stories that have room for a future.
hope.practice: Tell someone — or yourself, aloud — one true story of something damaged that recovered through care: a forest after a fire, a friendship after a quarrel.

quote.text: It matters what stories make worlds, what worlds make stories.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

nostalgia.text: A creaky step in the stairwell, the smell of your mother's wardrobe — new materialism takes such things seriously. Nostalgia is a longing for places and things that are no longer what they were, and its roots are very material. Jane Bennett shows that objects are not passive carriers of memory but participants in our lives: an old mug, the smell of a home, a particular street really do affect us. If we follow this thought further, nostalgia is not just "a memory in your head" but a response to a real connection with the material world that has changed. In Donna Haraway's spirit, one could add that the past doesn't leave entirely: it goes on living in matter, in bodies, in stories. You can gently touch these traces — an object, a photograph, a recipe — and let them link the past with the present.
nostalgia.practice: Hold an object connected with what you miss — or recall it in detail: its weight, smell, texture. Hold it for a minute without trying to remember anything — let the thing do its own work.

craving.text: The chocolate bar at the checkout sits at eye level for a reason — Jane Bennett would say that things know how to call to us. A craving — a sharp "I want it right now" — can take you over completely, and it's not a matter of weak character. In Vibrant Matter she writes about "thing-power": matter — food, chemical substances, objects — is not passive; it really does act on us. For Bennett, a craving arises in an "assemblage" — made of the body, a substance, tiredness, advertising, a place, the time of day. This removes part of the shame: it isn't only "your weak will" that wants; the whole assemblage wants. But it also opens a possibility: you can change not your whole self but one element of the assemblage — the place, the time, what is near you. Sometimes that is enough for the wave to pass by.
craving.practice: When a craving comes, rearrange the assemblage: go into another room, step outside, or call someone. Then notice how the wave has changed.

addiction.text: Picture a spider's web: pull one thread and the whole web trembles. Addiction works in a similar way: it is not a moral failure but a loop that life has gradually been built into, and it is hard to get out of. Jane Bennett speaks of "distributive agency" — the idea that action rarely belongs to a single "I": it is spread across an assemblage of body, substances, habits, places, people, the economy. In addiction, this whole network is acting, and that is why willpower alone is often not enough. At the same time, Bennett doesn't remove the person from the picture: we are one of the nodes in the network and can influence how it is arranged. Donna Haraway adds the notion of "response-ability" — the capacity to respond, which grows not alone but in kinship with others. In other words, getting out of the loop is not a heroic battle with yourself but a gradual reassembling: new places, new rhythms, new connections.
addiction.practice: Choose one thread of the web you can strengthen today: reach out to someone you trust, or look up the nearest mutual-help group meeting. Getting out of the loop is a reassembling done together with others.

hangover.text: We too are made of matter, Jane Bennett reminds us, and the morning after a heavy night you feel it especially: an aching body, anxiety, shame, gaps in memory. It's a hard morning, and you deserve gentleness. She writes that a human being is also in many ways "non-human": chemistry, microbes and minerals are at work in us, and they affect how we feel and think. In effect, part of the morning anxiety and the dark thoughts is the voice of a body that is recovering, not a final verdict on you. Your mood right now is shaped not only by what you did yesterday but also by what is happening in your body today. So you can treat it like weather: wait it out, take care of your body, and pass no verdicts on yourself until it changes.
hangover.practice: Treat the morning like weather: open a window, drink some water, take a warm shower. And tell yourself: "Right now my body is speaking, not only my conscience."

euphoria.text: Jane Bennett writes about moments when the world suddenly takes your breath away — and defends them against those who find rapture naive. A burst of euphoria is such a moment: the world seems open, you seem capable of anything, and there's no need to hurry to "bring it down to earth". In The Enchantment of Modern Life she argues with the familiar idea that the modern world is "disenchanted" and dull. She believes that moments of thrilling uplift and wonder are a real part of life, and they are valuable: such moments give energy, generosity, a desire to connect with the world. Then euphoria too is born in an assemblage — of body, light, people, music, events. This is useful to remember: the high is not only your personal "charge" but a fortunate convergence of circumstances that arrived and will, in its own time, change. You can rejoice in it fully — and notice what it was made of.
euphoria.practice: Write down what this high is made of, like a recipe: who was there, what was around, what was playing, what happened. A recipe won't repeat the miracle, but it will help you recognise yourself on other days.

crash.text: In the morning the campfire holds the same embers, but no fire: it lived while wood, air and people came together. A sharp drop after a celebration or a success is like that morning, and there is nothing shameful in it. Mood, as Jane Bennett writes, arises in an "assemblage" — made of the body, people, events, place. The party is over, people have gone home, the body is tired — the assemblage has come apart, and with it has gone the state it was holding. The drop is not proof that the high was "fake", and it is not the truth about your life. Donna Haraway calls on us to "stay with the trouble" — to flee neither into despair nor into hope of instant rescue, but to be in the present. You can stay with the drop in the same way: notice it, let your body recover, and little by little put together a new, calm assemblage of ordinary days.
crash.practice: Put together a "recovery assemblage" from at least one element: a warm meal, a short walk or a conversation with someone. One is enough for today.

panic.text: Jane Bennett insists that things are never just background: they are always doing something with us. In panic this knowledge becomes a support, because inside it is truly frightening: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, and it seems something irreparable is about to happen. Such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes, though from the inside that is hard to believe. New materialism offers a particular support here — the matter around you. When a storm rages inside, the world of things stays close: the floor holds your weight, the chair supports your back, the cup cools your palm. It follows that you can lean not on a thought but on these material connections — literally. You are not alone with your body: you are part of an assemblage that includes the ground under your feet, the air, and objects ready to support you.
panic.practice: Press your palms against a table or a wall and feel the thing push back. Take a few out-breaths longer than the in-breaths and name aloud five objects around you and their textures: smooth, cold, rough.

dread.text: The physicist Karen Barad shows that even the vacuum in quantum theory isn't empty: it flickers with possibilities. Existential dread — "what's the point of it all", the thought of finitude, the abyss underfoot — is heavy, and there's nothing shameful in it. New materialism doesn't promise a ready answer to the question of meaning, but it changes the picture itself. Barad writes that we don't stand "outside" the world, staring into a void: we are part of the world, entangled with it at every moment. If we follow this thought further, the abyss is not the whole truth: you are already woven into a fabric where something responds to you. Donna Haraway calls us "mortal critters", entangled with others, and sees in this not a sentence but a ground for care and kinship. Meaning here is not a conclusion but a connection you can feel.
dread.practice: Sit silently for a minute and follow a single breath: the air entering you now was just in leaves, in someone's lungs, in the wind. You are already woven into the world — literally.

fomo.text: Look at your palm: you see it from here, from this distance, with these eyes — and no other way. For Donna Haraway this simple fact holds the key to the fear of missing out, the feeling that everyone lives more interestingly and you are not where you should be. In her famous essay "Situated Knowledges" she criticises what she calls "the god trick" — the illusion that one can see everything at once from nowhere, from on high, without being in any particular place. A social media feed creates a similar illusion: it seems you are surveying all of life at once and missing what matters everywhere. But for Haraway every real view is "situated": it always comes from somewhere — from a particular body, place and history. The new materialists would probably say that there is no "right place"; there is your place — and it is no worse than others, simply the only one from which you can truly see and take part.
fomo.practice: Name aloud three details of your "here" that are in no feed: a smell, a sound, the light from the window. This is your situated view — the only one from which you can take part.

sleepless.text: Jane Bennett would say that sleep can't be ordered, only invited. At three in the morning, when the world seems asleep and you are left alone with circling thoughts, it's easy to forget this and start blaming yourself. For Bennett, sleep arises in an assemblage: body, light, temperature, noise, a screen, the events of the day, the worries we brought with us. If sleep doesn't come, it isn't your personal failure but an assemblage that hasn't come together yet. You don't have to fight yourself; you can gently change what is around you: a little darker, a little cooler, a little quieter. Donna Haraway would remind you that the night is full of life: plants breathe, animals roam, somewhere other people are awake too. You are not alone in this night — you are part of its breathing.
sleepless.practice: Watch your breathing like a tide, with a palm resting on your belly. In your mind, list those who are also awake tonight: an owl, a night watchman, the surf.

betrayal.text: Donna Haraway says that kinship can't simply be had — it is made every day, like bread. That is why betrayal wounds so deeply: someone you trusted stopped making your shared bond. Haraway writes a great deal about "response-ability" — the capacity to respond to another, to answer for a bond. In effect, betrayal is a rupture of response-ability: the other stopped responding to your bond as it required. The responsibility for this rupture does not lie with you. And your own capacity to respond, to trust and to care has not gone anywhere — it is still yours. Haraway reminds us that webs of kinship can be wide: beyond one person there are friends, family, animals, places. You can lean on these threads while the wound heals.
betrayal.practice: Lean your palm against a tree trunk, the wall of your home or the back of a sleeping cat — on something that holds you reliably. Stay like that for a minute, recalling the bonds that haven't broken.

jealousy.text: A lichen is a fungus and an alga that have lived together so long they have become one being. In closeness we grow together too, which is why jealousy is agonising: fear of loss, pain and anger twist into a tight knot. It follows that this feeling is understandable: we really are entangled with those we love — not metaphorically, but with our whole lives, habits, bodies. Donna Haraway suggests looking at relationships as "kinship", which is created and sustained by attention rather than owned by someone like a thing. A bond, in her view, lives in mutual response. Through this lens, you can listen to jealousy as a message about how much this bond matters to you — and notice that it cannot be held by force, but it can be sustained by attention and conversation. And one more thing: you are woven into more than one thread. Your life rests on a whole web of connections.
jealousy.practice: When you feel ready, say to your partner not "where were you?" but "our bond matters to me, let's talk about it." Notice how the conversation changes when it is about the thread rather than the suspicion.

resentment.text: Tense shoulders, a clenched jaw, thoughts that keep returning to one scene — new materialism holds that resentment lives right there, almost literally. An old grievance is a pain you carry for years, and you really were treated unfairly. Jane Bennett, with her idea of "distributive agency" — the thought that action is spread across many participants — shows that events are rarely created entirely by one person: circumstances, histories, pressures and webs of relations take part in them. Mind you, this doesn't remove responsibility from the person who hurt you, but it lets you loosen a little the knot in which all the pain is tied to one figure. And Karen Barad writes that the past is never finally closed: its meaning keeps changing in the present. Resentment does not have to remain an unchanging burden.
resentment.practice: Find where in your body the resentment lives — in your chest, shoulders, jaw. Rest your palm there and take a few slow out-breaths, as if easing a stiff muscle.

heartbreak.text: Two trees that grow side by side for years intertwine their roots so that only a wound can separate them. A breakup feels similar — as if part of you has been torn out, and new materialism doesn't consider this an exaggeration. Donna Haraway says that we don't exist on our own but "become-with": in relationships we really do shape each other — habits, pet phrases, rhythms, even the way we move and eat. Karen Barad calls this "intra-action": the partners in a relation don't exist ready-made before it; they emerge within it. So when the bond breaks, you change too: it isn't only memory that hurts but the whole familiar order of life, bodily and everyday. But what took shape in you during the relationship doesn't vanish — it remains yours. And the capacity to "become-with" remains too; in its own time it will find new connections — with people, places, pursuits.
heartbreak.practice: Say aloud one thing you learned in this relationship that will stay with you — a habit, a turn of phrase, a skill. This is the part of the tangle that is yours now.

impostor.text: A Catholic childhood, biology, feminism, dog sports — Donna Haraway is assembled from such different stories, and isn't ashamed of it. Impostor syndrome is the opposite fear: that you're about to be exposed and everyone will see you're "not the real thing". In A Cyborg Manifesto she gives up the dream of a "pure", whole, natural identity: we are all hybrids, assembled from different histories, skills, accidents and other people's influences. Her idea of "situated knowledges" — all knowledge is partial and always looks from somewhere — means that no one sees or knows everything. If we follow this thought further, the "real" expert who knows everything and depends on no one simply doesn't exist. Your feeling that "I'm put together from bits and pieces and there's a lot I don't know" is not an exposure but an honest description of how all knowledge works. Haraway prefers this honest incompleteness to the pose of an all-knowing goddess.
impostor.practice: Tell yourself aloud the story of your skill: whom you learned from, what you tried, where you went wrong. Listen — this is not a fake but an assemblage.

quote.text: I would rather be a cyborg than a goddess.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

self_hatred.text: Your inner critic speaks of you as if you were a statue that can be judged as a whole — whereas new materialism sees a person more as a living garden. Self-hatred is exhausting, and it's important to say straight away: the critic's verdict is not the truth about you. The critic speaks as if you were a separate, fully self-sufficient "I" that alone answers for everything that happens to it. But Jane Bennett and other new materialists show that we are assemblages: a body, a history, an environment, the people around us, the circumstances we grew up in. Rosi Braidotti, who is close to this current, speaks of an "affirmative" ethics: not negating the life in yourself but supporting its capacity to act and to rejoice. The new materialists would probably say that you deserve not judgement but care — the same care you would give any living creature.
self_hatred.practice: Imagine the critic saying these words about a plant you look after. What would you answer? Say the same thing to yourself — aloud or in a whisper.

helplessness.text: How much does one contribution weigh? Jane Bennett answers with stories of inconspicuous creatures that change the world without knowing it. Helplessness is a heavy feeling, when it seems that nothing depends on you. New materialism admits that in vast networks — the economy, the climate, politics — no single person really controls everything. But this thought has another side. In Vibrant Matter, Jane Bennett recalls Darwin's studies of earthworms: tiny creatures, each almost invisible, create the fertile layer of soil over centuries. In a distributed network, action is made up of many small contributions. Donna Haraway warns both against "there's nothing to be done anymore" and against waiting for a miraculous rescue: both moods lead us away from the present. In other words, your small action is not nothing but part of a large assemblage. Being powerless before the whole doesn't cancel the fact that your contribution, like the work of those unnoticed creatures, also keeps the earth alive.
helplessness.practice: Step out for a couple of minutes to the nearest lawn or flowerbed and look closely at the soil: somewhere in there Darwin's worms are at work. Then choose one very small action of your own for today.

procrastination.text: Some things dig in their heels: a drawer that sticks, a file you don't want to open — Jane Bennett takes their resistance seriously. Procrastination is when a task hangs over you and you can't get started, and shame piles on top. New materialism suggests you stop seeing this as purely a problem of will. Bennett writes that things have a power of their own: they dig in their heels, resist, attract or repel. A task is not only a thought in your head but a whole assemblage: the desk, the screen, a tired body, notifications, an unclear first step, the memory of past failures. If the assemblage doesn't come together into work, it isn't necessarily "laziness". Donna Haraway speaks of "sympoiesis" — "making-with": nothing is made alone. In effect, instead of pressuring yourself you can reassemble the circumstances: change your place, remove one distracting thing, invite someone to work alongside you. Sometimes what helps you start is not willpower but allies.
procrastination.practice: Call in an ally: ask someone to sit with you while you work — in person or on a video call — or simply move the task to a different place. Then take the smallest first step.

uprooted.text: Rosi Braidotti was born in Italy, grew up in Australia, studied in Paris and taught in Utrecht — and turned that life into a nomad's philosophy. Being cut off from home — emigration, a move, the ground slipping from under your feet — is a hard experience, and homesickness is legitimate. New materialism treats it with understanding, because it takes our connection to places seriously: the air, the landscape, the food, the sounds of your home street really were part of you. In Nomadic Subjects, Braidotti describes a "nomadic" identity — not as a loss of self but as a way of being yourself in motion, gathering connections in each new place. Donna Haraway speaks of "kinship" that is made, not only inherited. Then roots are not only what was left behind but also something you can put down anew: getting to know the trees on your street, the birds, the neighbours, the smells of a new place.
uprooted.practice: Choose one "resident" of your new place — a tree, a bird, a house along the way — and visit it on a walk today, as you would a new acquaintance.

overload.text: When more current flows into a grid than it can carry, the fuses trip — and that is not a breakdown but protection. Overload from news, messages and an endless feed is draining, and it says nothing about your weakness. In Vibrant Matter, Jane Bennett examines the great North American blackout of 2003: a vast power grid in which many elements — wires, stations, markets, flows of current — interacted in such a way that the system broke down. Bennett shows that networks have a life of their own that no one fully controls. Through this lens, your attention is also part of such a network: devices, apps and algorithms act on you, sometimes faster than you can decide anything. Tiredness from the stream is a signal of overload, like that of the power grid. Protecting yourself is not a matter of self-reproach but of reassembling: fewer incoming streams, more pauses and slow, tangible things.
overload.practice: Put your phone face down and for two minutes hold something slow and heavy — a stone, a mug, an apple. Notice its weight and temperature.

unreality.text: According to quantum physics, when you touch a cup you never quite touch it: a gap remains between the atoms — from this paradox Karen Barad draws a whole philosophy of touch. When the world or you yourself seem unreal, it is as if this gap had become noticeable, and that is a strange, unsettling experience. For her, reality is not a fixed backdrop that we observe from outside but something that constantly emerges in interactions: in touches, encounters, responses. In her essay "On Touching" she shows that even a simple touch is a complex event in which the "I" and the world meet. It follows that the sense of reality is not a given but something sustained by connection, and it can weaken when connections become few. Jane Bennett calls on us to notice things attentively — their weight, texture, springiness. Reality can be brought back little by little through the body: by touching, listening, feeling temperature.
unreality.practice: Take an object in your hands and name aloud five of its qualities: weight, temperature, texture, colour, and the sound it makes when you tap it. Let reality come back through your palms.

awe.text: A dead rat, a glove and a bottle cap by a storm drain hardly seem a reason for awe — yet Jane Bennett opens her main book with them. Awe before mountains, stars, the sea or music is one of the deepest experiences. Bennett considers "enchantment" — a feeling of being surprised and caught up by the world — an important force: in her view, it nourishes generosity and the wish to care. At the start of Vibrant Matter she describes how one day in Baltimore she saw, by a storm drain grate, a glove, a mat of pollen, a dead rat, a bottle cap and a stick — and suddenly felt the strange liveliness of these things. Awe, then, is the moment when the matter of the world opens itself to you in all its power. It doesn't need to be explained or used. You can simply stay in it and let it change the way you see.
awe.practice: Stay for a minute with what filled you with awe, without taking photos. Then shift your gaze to something quite inconspicuous nearby — a pebble, a leaf — and look at it with the same attention.

relief.text: A bridge literally straightens after a heavy train has passed — the steel releases its strain, and engineers can measure it. Relief works in a similar way: the load you were carrying is lifted, and the body breathes out by itself. New materialism suggests taking this moment seriously, because relief is a very bodily event. Jane Bennett insists that we are material beings, and our states live not only in our thoughts: tension is held in the muscles, in the breath, in posture. Relief is the moment when this whole assemblage rearranges itself: the shoulders drop, the breath deepens, the world around becomes visible again. The new materialists would probably say that relief is not a trifle, nor a reason to go looking for a new worry right away. It is your body coming back to itself. You can live it fully and notice who and what helped it come: people, circumstances, chance, things.
relief.practice: Take a slow out-breath and go over the participants in this relief in your mind — people, circumstances, things, chance. Give each a nod.

calm.text: Thoreau spent two years in a cabin by Walden Pond, noting how the ice cracked in spring and how ants waged war on the woodpile. Calm is a rare and precious state: nothing is urgent, it's quiet inside. In other words, calm is not only an "inner" achievement but a fortunate assemblage: soft light, even breathing, a familiar mug, silence, a person or an animal nearby. Jane Bennett, who wrote a book about Thoreau, values his ability to notice the world around him attentively and unhurriedly. Such attention is calming in itself: you stop being only in your thoughts and find yourself among things and creatures. Donna Haraway would remind you that calm is almost always shared: plants breathe nearby, a cat sleeps, water flows. You can treasure it without analysing too much — simply noticing who and what is sharing it with you right now.
calm.practice: Sit still for a minute, like Thoreau by the pond, and silently name three things or creatures that are sharing this calm with you right now.

inspiration.text: "I contain multitudes," wrote Walt Whitman, and Jane Bennett saw in this line an exact description of inspiration. Inspiration is the moment when thoughts and images seem to arrive by themselves and you want to act. New materialism suggests understanding it almost literally: inspiration comes from outside. In Influx and Efflux she reflects on how the world constantly flows into us — through air, sounds, images, other people — and flows back out in our words and actions. Donna Haraway speaks of "sympoiesis" — "making-with": nothing is made alone; all creativity is shared with people, creatures and things. In effect, inspiration is not the exclusive merit of a lonely genius but a fortunate meeting of currents. You can rejoice in it and notice what exactly flowed into it — so that you can return to those sources again.
inspiration.practice: Read aloud a line that is feeding you right now — from a book, a song, a conversation — and straight away make one small "out-breath" into the world: a sketch, a sentence, a call.

quote.text: It matters what stories make worlds, what worlds make stories.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

schadenfreude.text: Rosi Braidotti suggests testing any feeling with one question: does it increase my power to live or diminish it? Schadenfreude — a small warm wave when something goes wrong for someone — does worse on this test than it seems, and shame usually follows right away. On its own, this feeling says little about what kind of person you are. Following Spinoza, she distinguishes sad passions, which diminish our power to live, from joyful ones, which increase it. She proposes an "affirmative ethics" — not denying dark feelings but transforming them. Then schadenfreude is joy, but joy borrowed from someone else's failure: it rests on a picture of the world as a competition, where another's loss is your gain. If you notice this picture, you can ask what your own life is missing if it feeds itself this way. The answer usually speaks of your tiredness or hurt, not of malice.
schadenfreude.practice: When you notice schadenfreude, breathe out and ask: which of my own needs just got some comfort — rest, recognition, justice? Name it silently in one word.

contempt.text: Donna Haraway teaches us to look at another twice: the first glance is almost always wrong. Contempt — a cold feeling that looks down from above — refuses precisely that second glance; it often defends against disappointment, powerlessness or the fear of turning out to be similar. In When Species Meet she draws attention to the word "respect": the Latin respicere means "to look back, to look again". For her, to respect is not to stop at the first glance but to notice the other again and again, their "significant otherness" — the ways they really are different, without being lesser for it. Through this lens, contempt is a gaze that has decided not to look again: the other is frozen in a single picture. You don't have to force yourself to love someone you despise. But you can notice that contempt hides the complexity of the world from you — and that behind it there is often pain of your own.
contempt.practice: Think of the person you despise and "look again": name one trait of theirs that doesn't fit your judgement.

disgust.text: First recoil, then look closer — Jane Bennett once went through exactly this at a storm drain in Baltimore. Disgust is a very bodily feeling: the body pulls away before you have time to think, and it doesn't make you a bad person. In Vibrant Matter she describes how she once saw some debris in a storm drain: a glove, a bottle cap, a stick, a dead rat. At first — the usual recoil. And then the things suddenly showed themselves as lively, strangely active participants in the world, and disgust mingled with wonder. Bennett doesn't ask us to love trash; she shows that the line between "clean" and "vile" is largely drawn by us. It follows that disgust is the body's signal about a boundary it wants to hold. It deserves respect. But sometimes you can make out something else behind it — vulnerability, fear, even curiosity.
disgust.practice: Take a step back and one calm out-breath — let your body hold its boundary. Then, if it's safe, look again and name what you notice besides disgust: fear, surprise, curiosity.

revenge.text: When a bridge collapses, engineers look not for a single villain but for a chain: metal, weather, load, someone's cost-cutting. Jane Bennett looks at the hurt behind revenge the same way: you were treated unfairly, and you want the person who hurt you to feel pain too. This feeling doesn't make you cruel — it speaks of how deeply you were hurt. If we follow this thought further, revenge rests on a simplification: as if all the harm were gathered in one person, and if you strike at them, the world will be set level. Bennett doesn't cancel responsibility, but she widens the picture. Then you can hear the wish for revenge as a demand for justice and protection — and ask what would truly restore your footing. The feeling remains yours; you don't have to act on it by causing harm.
revenge.practice: Clench your fists as hard as you can for five seconds — and slowly open them. Ask yourself: if justice were restored, what would I feel? Listen to what this part of you wants.

anger_at_loved.text: Donna Haraway doesn't romanticise kinship: a dog can bite, a family can drive you to shouting, and it is still kinship. Anger at those close to you — a partner, parents, children — can be very strong, and then comes the shame, though anger doesn't cancel love. She insists that kinship is not harmony but "trouble": a living, difficult, tangled bond in which collisions are inevitable. Jane Bennett adds that our state is produced by an assemblage: hunger, lack of sleep, noise, a long day, small things piling up. The new materialists would probably say that an evening outburst at someone you love is not a verdict on your relationship or the truth about you, but an event in which many things took part. This doesn't remove the wish to make things right, but it helps you do so without punishing yourself. Anger can show where you yourself are short of care.
anger_at_loved.practice: Once you've cooled down, say one sentence to them about the assemblage rather than about them: "I was hungry and worn out, and I snapped at you." It's not an excuse but an honest picture.

ambivalence.text: Donna Haraway's cyborg lives calmly on both sides of a boundary at once: human and machine, nature and culture. Loving a person and at the same time being unable to stand them is hard, and it seems you must finally decide which is true. Haraway suggests not rushing to choose. In A Cyborg Manifesto she rejects the familiar binary divisions — nature or culture, body or mind, self or other — and values irony as the ability to hold incompatible things together. In other words, your mixed feelings are not a mistake and not a sign that the love is "fake". Someone close to you is not a simple object but a living tangle, and your bond with them is a tangle too: it holds tenderness, irritation and history. Both sides can be true at once. To admit this is to stop waging war on yourself.
ambivalence.practice: Take an object in each hand — one warm, one cool — and hold them at the same time. In the same way you can hold tenderness and irritation, without choosing.

quote.text: Irony is about contradictions that do not resolve into larger wholes, even dialectically, about the tension of holding incompatible things together because both or all are necessary and true.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

guilty_relief.text: A muscle that has held a weight for months trembles when it is finally released — not from whim but from physiology. Relief after a breakup, after someone's death, or after the end of a loved one's long illness often comes with shame, but relief and love get along perfectly well. Long caregiving, worry, sleepless nights — this is tension that has lived for months in the muscles, the breath, sleep. When it goes, the body breathes out by itself, without asking permission. Karen Barad speaks of "entanglement": what is truly connected doesn't come untangled simply because circumstances have changed. In effect, your bond with the person doesn't vanish because things have become easier for you. Relief is not betrayal but a sign of how heavy the load was. You can allow yourself both.
guilty_relief.practice: Tell yourself, with a hand on your chest: "I feel lighter, and I still love." Stay with this for a minute.

indifference.text: Every torch's battery runs down, and no torch is to blame for the dark — Donna Haraway would say that responding also takes resources. Sometimes something happens that "should" move you — someone else's grief, an important event — and inside it is quiet. And on top of the indifference comes anxiety: "is something wrong with me?" Haraway speaks of "response-ability" — the capacity to respond. But for her every response is situated: it is born in a particular body, at a particular moment, with a particular store of strength. Jane Bennett adds that the capacity to be enchanted and to feel compassion is not a permanent property of the soul but a state that depends on the assemblage: tiredness, overload, how much you have already been through. Then indifference is not proof of callousness but a sign that your capacity to respond is exhausted for now. Feelings often come back later, when there is room for them.
indifference.practice: Let your capacity to respond recharge: sit in silence with your eyes closed for five minutes, without reading the news or checking whether your feelings are back.

escape.text: A hermit crab changes shells when the old one gets too tight — and no one calls it running away. The wish to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — and go somewhere no one knows you can be very strong. It is legitimate: this is often the voice of something that has long had no room. Jane Bennett sees life as an "assemblage" — made of people, places, things, rhythms, obligations. Some assemblages hold us up; others slowly drain us. Through this lens, the wish to run away is not a whim but a signal that your current assemblage has stopped holding you. Donna Haraway, speaking of the difficulties of our time, suggests "staying with the trouble" — throwing yourself neither into despair nor into a dream of instant rescue, but carefully working out what is happening. This doesn't mean leaving is not allowed. It means you can first understand which part of the assemblage exactly you want to be free of.
escape.practice: Imagine you are a hermit crab: which part of the shell pinches most — one specific part, not your whole life? Name it aloud.

forbidden_attraction.text: A magnet doesn't choose what to be drawn to — Jane Bennett and Karen Barad insist that attraction is older than human will. Attraction to someone who is "off limits" — an unavailable person, or the "wrong" one — often brings turmoil and shame, as if the feeling itself were already a wrongdoing. But attraction doesn't ask permission, and it says little about your decency. New materialism takes the force of attraction seriously. Jane Bennett writes about "thing-power" — the world's capacity to seize and draw us in — and Karen Barad says that desire and yearning belong to matter itself, not only to our "corrupt" will. It follows that attraction is the force of an encounter passing through you, not an order you are obliged to carry out or suppress. You can approach it with curiosity: what exactly about this person makes you feel so alive? Often the answer says more about your own life than about them.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Imagine yourself as a magnet and ask: what exactly in this person pulls — which quality? Name it and think about where else in your life it might be found.

social_anxiety.text: Two dancers aren't a couple before the dance — the couple appears as they move; this is how Karen Barad sees every encounter. Fear of people and their judgement — stiffness, a burning face, the wish to become invisible — is very draining, and you are not alone in it. Barad calls this "intra-action": the participants in an encounter don't exist as ready-made, separate figures who then collide — they take shape within the interaction itself. If we follow this thought further, in a conversation there is no fixed judge and no fixed defendant: you are not being "assessed" as a finished thing; together with others you create a situation in which they too are nervous and they too don't know things. And Jane Bennett would remind you that the body is a full participant: a pounding heart and a trembling voice are not "weakness of character" but the body's own reaction. It can be met gently, not with reproach.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, tell yourself: "The other person is feeling something right now too" — and in the conversation ask them one question about themselves. An encounter takes two.

uncertainty.text: Niels Bohr argued with Einstein for thirty years and never gave way: the world, for Bohr, is not settled in advance. Uncertainty — not knowing what will happen — is draining: the mind tries again and again to calculate everything in advance. Karen Barad, a physicist and philosopher, follows Niels Bohr in showing that indeterminacy is not simply a shortfall in our knowledge. For her it is a feature of reality itself: much is not settled in advance but becomes determinate only in the course of interactions. In her essay "Situated Knowledges", Donna Haraway adds that it is impossible to see everything at once from above — all knowledge is partial and made from somewhere. The new materialists would probably say that you don't have to know the future in order to act honestly. Uncertainty is not your personal failure at forecasting but part of how the world is made. There is less threat in it if you remember: not yet decided also means still open.
uncertainty.practice: Say aloud: "I don't know what will happen with…, but right now I know that…" — and finish the second part with one fact about the present: what is underfoot, who is near, what is in your hands.

quote.text: Only partial perspective promises objective vision.
quote.author: Donna Haraway

waiting.text: Dough rises in the dark under a towel, and peeking won't make it any faster: the yeast is doing the work. Waiting — for results, an answer, news — is one of the most drawn-out states: time stretches, and it's hard to get on with anything else. Jane Bennett speaks of "distributive agency": almost any outcome is produced by many participants at once — people, machines, procedures, bodies, weather. In other words, while you wait, things are not standing still: somewhere lab analysers are running, letters are being read, a decision is taking shape. It's just that this part of the assemblage isn't in your hands right now. Donna Haraway loves images of slow processes — growth, ripening, compost — in which much happens invisibly. Waiting is agonising partly because it seems to us that everything depends on our straining. Acknowledging that others are acting now is not passivity but an honest picture, in which you can loosen your grip a little.
waiting.practice: Give your hands a slow task that also involves waiting: water a plant, put the kettle on and stay until it boils. Let someone else — water, fire — do the work for you.

regret.text: In the quantum "eraser" experiment it seems possible to change what a particle "did" earlier — Karen Barad takes this puzzle seriously. Regret over something done or not done can come back again and again: "if only I had…" This feeling speaks of what mattered to you. Reflecting on such experiments, Barad offers an unexpected thought: the past is not closed once and for all. She stresses that its traces are not erased — what was done stays done. But what the past turns out to be keeps taking shape in new interactions: its meaning, consequences and connections are not yet complete. In effect, regret is not only longing for what cannot be brought back but also taking part in what the past will become. You can't replay that moment, but you can influence what grows out of it — including through how you treat it now.
regret.practice: Write down one regret, and beneath it: "What could grow out of this now is…" — and add one small possibility.

longing.text: Two particles that were once linked remain "entangled" even when carried far apart — Karen Barad sees more than physics in this. Longing for a particular person — their voice, their smell, the way they laugh — can be almost physical, and that is no exaggeration. New materialism takes seriously the fact that feelings live in matter: in the body, in things, in places. Then your longing is not being "stuck" but living evidence of how entangled you are with this person: your habits, pet phrases, even gestures carry their trace. Longing reminds you of a bond that keeps acting even at a distance. You don't have to drive it away; you can cherish it as a sign that the meeting was real.
longing.practice: Today, do one thing the way this person would — their turn of phrase, a gesture, their way of making tea. Let the bond work across the distance.

quote.text: Matter feels, converses, suffers, desires, yearns and remembers.
quote.author: Karen Barad
quote.source: interview in New Materialism: Interviews & Cartographies (2012)

world_pain.text: Coral, mycelium, a flock of starlings — Donna Haraway looks for images of life held up by the many, not by a lone hero. Pain for the world — wars, disasters, injustice — can overwhelm you so much that it's hard to live your own life. This pain is legitimate: it speaks of your connection with others. Rosi Braidotti, who is close to new materialism, puts it this way: we are all in this together, but we are not one and the same. Suffering is unequally distributed, and your pain is a response to someone else's, not a copy of it. Braidotti proposes an "affirmative ethics" — neither denying pain nor drowning in it, but transforming it into a capacity to act together with others. Donna Haraway would add that "staying with the trouble" means not turning away, but also not demanding that you carry the whole world alone. Your part of the response can be small and still be real.
world_pain.practice: Do one small act of response within your strength — help, support, talk — and one act of care for yourself. A starling in a flock doesn't have to fly for everyone.

rejection.text: Where does a cloud end? Karen Barad would answer: where we drew the line looking at it just now — and at another moment it would run differently. Rejection wounds painfully: it seems a verdict has been passed on you — "you don't fit". Barad calls this an "agential cut": the boundaries between "ours" and "theirs", "inside" and "outside" are not given in advance but are drawn in specific interactions — here and now, under these conditions. It follows that rejection is one such cut, made in one situation, by one person or group. It is real and painful, but it is not the final truth about your essence. In other encounters, under other conditions, the boundary will fall differently. New materialism in general doubts that a person has an unchanging essence that anyone could definitively judge. You are an ongoing process, and a single "no" doesn't bring it to an end.
rejection.practice: Go today to where the line runs differently — to a friend, to a community where you are welcome — or at least call. One "no" is one cut, not the whole map.

abandonment.text: A mushroom is only a small part of a mycelium stretching for hundreds of metres underground, held by countless threads. The fear of being abandoned can be sharp and clinging: every silence from someone close seems like the beginning of the end, and behind it is the wish for a secure bond. Donna Haraway loves the image of string figures — the children's game in which a pattern passes from hand to hand: one holds, another picks it up, and the figure lives as long as it is passed on. If we follow this thought further, the fear of abandonment is especially strong when your whole figure is held by a single pair of hands. But you can also notice the other threads — friends, places, pursuits, animals — that also hold the pattern of your life. The more of them there are, the less each pause feels like a break.
abandonment.practice: Draw yourself as a dot and run threads to everyone and everything that holds you right now — people, places, activities, animals. Look at your mycelium.

unrequited.text: Training with her dog, Donna Haraway came to see that even the most beloved creature remains truly other, with a will of its own. Unrequited love hurts in a particular way: the feeling is enormous, and there is no answer. In The Companion Species Manifesto she speaks of "significant otherness": the other is not a mirror of our desires but a truly different being with their own life, rhythm and choices. To love is to meet this otherness, including the possibility that it may not answer us in kind. It follows that unrequitedness is not a verdict on your worth but an encounter with the other's freedom. And new materialism would add: your feeling doesn't become any less real because of this. It really acts in you, changes you, opens you. You can grieve for what didn't happen and at the same time respect the fact that you are capable of loving like this.
unrequited.practice: Write: "My love has taught me…" — and finish it with one discovery about yourself that it brought.

humiliation.text: A fungus, a worm, a human, a river — in Donna Haraway's world they are all participants in one story, and no one stands a rung lower. Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: it is as if you had been pushed lower than you are. This pain is legitimate, and the blame for the humiliation does not lie with you. In A Cyborg Manifesto she shows that the familiar pairs of "higher and lower" — mind and body, human and animal, culture and nature — have served a logic of domination: someone is always placed above and someone below. In other words, humiliation is an attempt to force you onto the bottom rung of a ladder that doesn't really exist in the world. It wounds, but it doesn't determine your place. Your dignity doesn't depend on whoever tried to take it away.
humiliation.practice: Say aloud to yourself: "What was done to me is about them and the situation, not about my worth." Then stand up and feel the floor holding you on a level with everything else.

body_shame.text: A mirror shows only the surface, while beneath it, this very second, a heart is beating, a scratch is healing, breakfast is being digested. Dissatisfaction with your body can be a constant background — from childhood we are taught to see the body as a shop window — and new materialism offers a different view. In Vibrant Matter, Jane Bennett reminds us that the body is a community: billions of bacteria live in it, and countless processes you never think about are at work. In A Cyborg Manifesto, Donna Haraway gives up the dream of a "pure", "natural", ideal body: we are all hybrids. In effect, the body is not a picture to be rated but a living assemblage that every day breathes, digests, repairs itself and carries you through the world. You don't have to love every feature of it, and you can still respect what it does.
body_shame.practice: Rest your palm on your chest and feel your body breathing and beating right now, asking nothing of you. Name three things it has done for you today.

illness.text: The immune system is not an army but rather a noisy city of negotiations, Donna Haraway suggests. Illness, when the body lets you down, is a hard experience: it hurts, it's frightening, and often a grudge against your own body appears. These feelings are legitimate. In her essay on "the biopolitics of postmodern bodies", Donna Haraway examined how often the body and immunity are spoken of in the language of war: "fighting", "enemies", "defeat". Such language quietly turns the ill person into a loser. Then the body is not a machine commanded by the will and not a battlefield, but a living assemblage of many participants, not all of whom obey us. Illness is not your fault and not a betrayal by your body, but an event that is happening to you and in you. You can treat your body as an ally in a difficult time, not as a culprit.
illness.practice: Rest your palm on the part of your body that is struggling right now and silently say: "We're going through this together."

pride.text: An orchestra plays as a whole, and yet after the concert the violinist may be proud of their part — new materialism agrees. Pride in something you've done is a good, deserved feeling; there's no need to hide it. New materialism is sometimes understood as dissolving personal merit: if assemblages do the acting, there's nothing to be proud of. But Jane Bennett is saying something else. For her, action is distributed — people, tools and circumstances take part in it — and your role in this assemblage is entirely real. You were the node where everything came together; you chose, persisted, invested yourself. Acknowledging the other participants doesn't take away your contribution; it makes your pride calmer and warmer: there is less rivalry in it and more joy that things worked out. Through this lens, you can be proud with all your heart and at the same time thank those who helped. One doesn't get in the way of the other.
pride.practice: Tell someone about your result in two parts: "My contribution was that I…" and "I was helped by…". Pride and gratitude sound fine together.

melancholy.text: A fallen leaf on wet asphalt still keeps the curve of the branch it hung from — Jane Bennett knows how to see a whole story in such things. Gentle sadness, melancholy, is a quiet, slightly sad and yet warm state, and it doesn't need fixing. New materialism invites you to see in it not only an "inner" mood but an encounter with the world. Jane Bennett writes that mood is made up of many participants: light, weather, sounds, smells, memories, the body. Autumn light, rain outside the window, an old song really do take part in your melancholy — it is made together with them. Bennett also values quiet forms of enchantment: not rapture, but an attentive, slightly sad stillness before the fragility of things. It follows that melancholy is a way of feeling especially finely that everything passes and is therefore precious. You can simply stay in it, as in good weather.
melancholy.practice: Go outside for a few minutes and find one fragile thing — a leaf, a puddle, a reflection in a window. Stay with it until it changes.
